draft.title: Material and non-material living standards
card: how well off people in a country are. They cover how much people can buy and also the quality of their lives.
access to goods and services, such as food, housing, clothing, healthcare and transport. GDP per person is the common way to measure it.
things that are not bought or sold directly, such as a clean environment, good health, safety, literacy and leisure time.
Income can rise while non-material living standards fall. For example, a mining boom may lift incomes but add pollution to a town's air.
draft.remember: Living standards include what people can buy and the quality of life around them.

a.q: Which change would raise non-material living standards in a city?
opts: Cleaner air in a large city
A rise in the average nurse wage
More new cars sold to households
a.why: Cleaner air is part of the environment, which is not bought or sold directly, so it is non-material. The other three are about income or access to goods and services, which are material.
a.clue: Look for the change that is not about income or buying things.

b.q: Average income in Bendigo rises 10%, but workers now work much longer hours and have less free time. What happens to living standards?
b.why: Higher income raises material living standards because people can buy more. Less free time is a non-material loss, so non-material living standards fall. Choosing both rise treats income as the whole picture and ignores the lost free time.
b.clue: Free time is on one side and income is on the other.

a.best: Cleaner air in a large city
